name: Maintenance planning and scheduling
summary: Every week the maintenance planners turn PMs falling due, inspection findings and backlog work requests into a schedule for the mechanics, millwrights and electricians on site. They screen and plan jobs, check and order parts, read the mine and mill plans, and agree equipment release windows with operations before the superintendent freezes the schedule; supervisors then run it shift by shift and the planner measures how much was done. The schedule breaks most weeks because breakdowns pull people away, production keeps units it was meant to release, and parts promised for the week do not arrive.

baseline.org_archetype: A single-mine Canadian gold producer with one ramp-and-shaft underground mine, a 1,000 t/d class mill, about 300 employees on 14-on/14-off rotations living in camp, and a CMMS (ERP maintenance module) fed from paper work order cards.
baseline.notes: Three planners on office hours plan for about 50 maintenance trades on 14/14 rotation; the schedule is kept in a spreadsheet beside the CMMS.

trigger: The weekly planning cycle starts on Monday from the backlog of work requests and the PMs due the following week.
end_state: The schedule week has been run, unfinished work returned to the backlog, and compliance reviewed by the maintenance superintendent.

volume.seasonality: One schedule every week; planning before a mill shutdown takes more time.

evidence.note: Weekly cycle; matches the organisation file.
About 27 planner hours per weekly cycle; the rest of the three planners' time goes to work order entry and shutdown planning.
Backlog review, weekly meeting, freeze and KPI review, about 4 hours a week.
Line-up assignment and break-in decisions, about 5-6 hours a week across four supervisors.
Chasing parts for planned jobs, about 2 hours a week.
Kitting planned jobs, about 4 hours a week.
Equipment release decisions at the weekly meeting.

systems.name: Maintenance management system (ERP maintenance module or standalone)
Mid-market ERP for finance, purchasing, inventory and fixed assets
Shift reports, line-up boards and production tallies (paper and spreadsheets)
Shared drives and document library (procedures, permits, drawings)
Leaky feeder radio and surface radio network
Mine design and scheduling software (3D design, scheduling)
Payroll and timekeeping service (outsourced payroll with site time entry)

steps.name: Sweep and screen new work requests
steps.description: On Monday the planner pulls every new work request from the CMMS and the paper request book: operator defect reports, inspection findings, PM defects and follow-ups from temporary breakdown fixes. Duplicates are merged and each request is checked for a unit number, location and clear description.

error.defect_description: A safety-related request is screened as low priority.

evidence.note: Weekly cycle described in hvi2026; times are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Clarify unclear requests
steps.description: For requests that say little more than 'fix leak', the planner looks at the equipment in the shop or phones the requester. Requesters who have gone out on rotation answer by email or not until they return.

error.defect_description: A request is closed as a duplicate when it is a separate fault.

evidence.note: 14-on/14-off rotations mean half the requesters are off site at any time; author's estimate.

steps.name: Review and prioritise the backlog
steps.description: The maintenance superintendent and the planner go through the backlog list in a short meeting, approve new requests, set priorities by safety and production consequence, and cancel stale ones.

error.defect_description: Priorities follow the loudest requester rather than consequence.

evidence.note: Backlog ageing buckets and approval before scheduling from umbrex; meeting length is the author's estimate.

steps.name: List PMs due next week
steps.description: The CMMS forecast lists the preventive work orders that fall due next week from the latest hour-meter readings and calendar intervals, for mobile equipment, fixed plant, electrical and hoist inspections.

error.defect_description: A PM is missing because its meter was not updated.

evidence.note: Weekly cycle described in hvi2026; times are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Plan the top corrective jobs
steps.description: For the highest-priority backlog jobs the planner writes the job scope and steps, estimates hours by trade, lists parts and special tools, notes permits (hot work, confined space, lockout points) and attaches drawings or manuals.

error.defect_description: Hours are underestimated or a part is left off the job plan.

evidence.note: Weekly cycle described in hvi2026; times are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Check parts and raise requisitions
steps.description: The planner checks stock for each planned job in the ERP, reserves what is on the shelf, and raises purchase requisitions for non-stock parts. Jobs without parts on site are marked not ready.

error.defect_description: A reservation is made for stock that is already committed to another job.

evidence.note: A job is not ready until its parts are on the shelf (hvi2026); times are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Chase parts for planned jobs
steps.description: The buyer turns the requisitions into orders and phones suppliers about open orders for jobs on next week's list, then gives the planner expected delivery dates.

error.defect_description: A promised date is optimistic and the job is scheduled without its parts.

evidence.note: Author's estimate for a three-planner maintenance group at a 40-unit underground fleet and 1,000 t/d class mill.

steps.name: Read the mine and mill plans for the week
steps.description: The planner reads the short-range mine plan and the mill run plan: which headings and stopes are active, which units are critical, when ore will be short and when the mill or hoist could stop without losing production.

error.defect_description: A critical unit's production need is missed.

evidence.note: Author's estimate for a three-planner maintenance group at a 40-unit underground fleet and 1,000 t/d class mill.

steps.name: Check who is on site next week
steps.description: The planner checks the rotation roster for mechanics, millwrights, electricians and welders on each crew, subtracting training, vacation and people lent to projects, to get the available hours by trade and shift.

error.defect_description: Training days are missed and the schedule is overloaded.

evidence.note: Author's estimate for a three-planner maintenance group at a 40-unit underground fleet and 1,000 t/d class mill.

steps.name: Draft the weekly schedule
steps.description: In the scheduling spreadsheet the planner assigns PMs and ready corrective jobs to days and crews, loading about 80% of available hours and leaving the rest for breakdowns, and lists the equipment release windows to request from operations.

error.defect_description: Two jobs needing the same unit or tradesperson are scheduled at once.

evidence.note: Loading 80-85% of crew hours (hvi2026) or freezing 70-80% (umbrex); times are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Hold the weekly planning meeting
steps.description: The maintenance superintendent takes the draft to the weekly meeting with the mine and mill superintendents and the mine captains, walks through the equipment release requests and plant stops, and hears production's objections.

evidence.note: Joint operations-maintenance review before the freeze; meeting length is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Confirm equipment releases
steps.description: The mine captain confirms which units can be released on which shifts given the production targets for the week. Units needed for a stope blast or a development push are often refused or moved.

evidence.note: Share of weeks with refused releases is the author's estimate; the organisation file notes that PM competes with production for machines.

steps.name: Re-sequence the schedule
steps.description: The planner moves refused jobs to other days or the following week, fills the gaps with other ready work and re-checks that tradespeople and parts still line up.

error.defect_description: A moved PM is forgotten and runs overdue.

evidence.note: Author's estimate for a three-planner maintenance group at a 40-unit underground fleet and 1,000 t/d class mill.

steps.name: Update the shutdown work list
steps.description: Jobs that need the mill, crusher or hoist stopped for more than a shift are moved onto the list for the next planned shutdown, and when a shutdown falls within the planning horizon the planner sends the list to the shutdown plan.

error.defect_description: A job that needs a plant stop is left on the weekly schedule.

evidence.note: Author's estimate for a three-planner maintenance group at a 40-unit underground fleet and 1,000 t/d class mill.

steps.name: Approve and freeze the schedule
steps.description: The maintenance superintendent signs off the schedule. After the freeze, changes need the superintendent's agreement except for safety and production-stopping breakdowns.

control.basis: Site schedule freeze rule: after sign-off only the maintenance superintendent may add or drop jobs, except for safety and production-stopping breakdowns

evidence.note: Freeze with a named approver for changes; time is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Issue the schedule and job packages
steps.description: The planner emails the schedule to supervisors, the mine and the mill, posts it in the shops and prints a package per day with work orders, job plans, checklists and parts lists.

error.defect_description: A job package is missing its checklist or drawing.

evidence.note: Weekly cycle described in hvi2026; times are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Kit and stage parts by day
steps.description: The warehouse attendants pick the reserved parts for each scheduled job, issue them to the work orders and stage them in labelled bins in the surface shop, underground bay and mill shop.

error.defect_description: A kit is staged in the wrong shop or a part is short.

evidence.note: Weekly cycle described in hvi2026; times are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Run the schedule at each shift line-up
steps.description: During the schedule week the maintenance supervisor on each shift assigns the day's work orders to crews at the line-up, checks parts and unit releases, and moves jobs when a unit is not released or a breakdown takes the crew.

error.defect_description: A scheduled job is dropped without being recorded as missed.

evidence.note: Weekly cycle described in hvi2026; times are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Decide on break-in work
steps.description: When breakdowns or urgent requests arrive the supervisor decides which scheduled jobs to drop to free a tradesperson, and records the break-ins on the schedule sheet.

error.defect_description: A PM is dropped repeatedly in favour of lower-priority work.

evidence.note: Break-ins should be limited to 10-15% of weekly hours; time is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Close out the week
steps.description: After the schedule week the planner collects the returned job packages and schedule sheets, marks each job done, partly done or not started, and carries unfinished work back to the backlog.

error.defect_description: Jobs done but not written up are carried over as not done.

evidence.note: Weekly cycle described in hvi2026; times are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Calculate schedule and PM compliance
steps.description: The planner calculates schedule compliance (jobs completed over jobs scheduled), PM compliance, break-in hours and backlog in crew-weeks in a spreadsheet and lists the main reasons jobs were missed.

error.defect_description: Partly completed jobs are counted as done.

evidence.note: Metric definitions from umbrex and hvi2026; time is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Review the week's results
steps.description: The maintenance superintendent reviews the KPI sheet with the supervisors and planner, agrees actions on repeat causes such as missing parts or refused releases, and carries the figures into the monthly report to the general manager.

evidence.note: umbrex gives 80-90% as typical of disciplined programmes; the 70% share of weeks below 80% is the author's estimate for 2019-2022 mid-size mines.

exceptions.name: Releases refused
exceptions.description: Production refuses key equipment releases and the planner re-sequences the week.

exceptions.name: Schedule sent back
exceptions.description: The superintendent sends the schedule back for changes before the freeze.

exceptions.name: Week below target
exceptions.description: Breakdowns, missing parts and refused releases leave schedule compliance under 80%.

evidence.note: Typical range given by both sources; not a mining measurement for 2019-2022.
Stated as a guideline.
Stated as a healthy range.

benchmarks.unit: calendar days from the Monday sweep to the post-week review

evidence.note: Planning week (Monday to Friday), the seven-day schedule week and a review early in the following week.

pain_points.description: Breakdowns pull tradespeople off scheduled work, and break-ins are rarely held to the 10-15% guideline.

evidence.note: Break-ins as the main driver of low schedule compliance.

pain_points.description: Production keeps units it was asked to release, so PMs slip and the week is re-planned.

evidence.note: The organisation file and author's estimate; no source for a rate was opened.

pain_points.description: Parts promised for the week do not arrive at a remote site, so jobs are scheduled that cannot be done.

evidence.note: Parts on the shelf as the readiness test.

pain_points.description: Requests are vague and requesters are off on rotation, so planners spend time chasing details.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

sources.title: Maintenance Compliance Rate
sources.supports: Weekly schedule compliance (completed scheduled work orders over scheduled work orders) of 80-90% in disciplined programmes; break-in work after the schedule freeze kept to 10-15% of weekly hours; freeze 70-80% of available hours with a joint operations-maintenance review; a site at 65% compliance can gain 15-20 points from a one-week freeze and a joint scheduling meeting; backlog ageing buckets 0-7, 8-14, 15-30 and 31+ days.

sources.title: Weekly Maintenance Scheduling for Mining Teams
sources.publisher: Heavy Vehicle Inspection & Maintenance (JRS Innovation Inc.)
sources.supports: Weekly cycle for mining maintenance: mid-week sweep of open work orders, defects and coming PMs; planning with hour estimates, parts and permits; a job is not ready until its parts are on the shelf; schedule loaded to 80-85% of crew hours and frozen after machine release windows are confirmed with operations; daily 15-minute check; end-of-week schedule compliance and break-in review; wrench time 25-35% without structured planning; healthy backlog 2-4 weeks; a 250-hour service on a truck running 5,000-7,000 hours a year comes due every two to three weeks. Published after the reference period; used as a description of common practice, not as a 2019-2022 measurement.

assumptions: The unit of work is one weekly schedule; the cycle runs from the Monday sweep through the schedule week to the review, so consecutive cycles overlap.
touch_min for planning steps is the total for the week (10-20 planned jobs and 15-20 PMs), not per job.

The organisation file lists only hse-inspections as a trigger; work requests also come from mine operators, mill operators, PM defects and breakdown follow-ups, so these are added with estimated shares.
The buyer, warehouse attendant and mine captain take part although the organisation file lists only planner, superintendent and supervisor.
hvi2026 was published in 2026 and is used only as a description of the weekly cycle, which was common practice in 2019-2022.
Loaded costs are the organisation file's.
